en: Now begins the Pulastya-smṛti,
concerning the description of the duties of the castes and stages of life:
at Kurukṣetra, the sages spoke to the high-souled Pulastya.
Tell us those dharmas and their various types according to the Smṛti tradition.
Thus questioned, he replied to all those sages who were asking:
"O best of the twice-born, listen to dharma as it exists in fivefold ways. (2)

The duty of the social classes (varṇadharma) is remembered as one; after that, the duties of the stages of life (āśramadharma); and thirdly, the duty based on qualities and circumstances (guṇanaimittika). ||3||
That authority which proceeds by relying upon a single caste is to be known as the duty of caste (varṇadharma), such as the initiation ceremony (upanayana) among the three [higher castes]. ||4||
Whatever object is established by depending upon a particular basis has been described; likewise, the duties of the stages of life (āśrama-dharma) include such things as alms and morsels of food.
That rule which proceeds by means of both [the agent and the action] is to be understood as "contingent" (naimittika), such as the rule for expiation (prāyaścitta). ||6||
The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and the mendicant—the duties of these stages of life have been declared; the duty of the king is the fifth.

The duty of the social classes (*varṇadharma*) pertaining to the four [classes], as well as that of the stages of life (*āśrama*), that which is common to both, and that which pertains to the remainder of the two. (8)
Sacrifices, study, and giving according to the scriptures are declared to be the eternal common duty of Brahmins, Kshatriyas, and Vaishyas. (9)

Sacrificing for others, teaching, and the protection of all beings are prescribed as the livelihood for a king; cattle-rearing and agriculture are likewise recorded as the means of subsistence for a Vaiśya. ||10||
For a Śūdra, service to the twice-born is the duty; for the twice-born, it is service according to their respective order.
Furthermore, the livelihood of a Śūdra consists of that service, as well as compassion and manual labor.
Dwelling with the guru, service to the sacred fire, Vedic study, observance of vows, bathing at the three times of day, and remaining with the guru until death for the sake of his servants. ||12||
In the absence of those, [one should seek it] from the son of the teacher, or likewise from a fellow student;
or by choice, equality [of status] may be attained, for such is the specific duty of a student.

Wearing a girdle, with matted hair, carrying a staff, or shaven-headed, he should take refuge in the house of his guru; otherwise, he may by his own choice become a householder or enter another stage of life.
The performance of the Agnihotra sacrifice, living by one's own duties, the giving of dharma, optional rites, and the selling of people everywhere—[these are forbidden]. (15)
O Devapitṛs! This dharma of the householder, which consists of the purificatory rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, is characterized by compassion for guests and all living beings. 16.

Wearing matted hair, maintaining the sacred fire, sleeping on the ground, wearing deerskins, dwelling in the forest, and subsisting on water, roots, wild rice, and grains—[these are the marks of a forest-dweller]. (17)
Abstaining from accepting gifts, bathing three times a day, maintaining silence, and honoring the deities and guests—this is the dharma of forest-dwellers. (18)
The renunciation of all undertakings, subsisting on alms-food, being rooted in a simple livelihood, freedom from possessiveness, absence of malice, and equanimity toward all living beings. ||19||
Embracing both the pleasant and the unpleasant, remaining unchanging in the face of pleasure and pain, purity both internal and external, self-restraint, and the performance of vows. ||20||
The withdrawal of all the senses, constancy in concentration and meditation, and likewise purity of being—this is called the dharma of the wandering mendicant. ||21||

Non-violence, truthfulness, honesty, purity, compassion, and forbearance are said to be the common dharma for those belonging to the social classes (varṇas) as well as those bearing the marks of religious orders (liṅgins). ||22||

One's own knowledge resides in the hearts of all those who bear the marks of the [four] castes and stages of life; this Dharma is declared to be twofold: that which has its purpose seen, and secondly, that which has its purpose unseen. ||23||
The third concerns the welfare of both, while the fourth is based on logic; the fifth involves non-prosecution of both parties, and the sixth is the imposition of punishment. ||24||
The optionality of things that serve the same purpose is proclaimed to be rooted in logic; however, Dharma as it is known in the Veda is exactly the same in the Smṛti. (25)
The wise maintain that the *anuvāka* and the *śrutisūkta* are for the sake of ritual action;
this present effort is for their purpose, and they should be cultivated by one who desires the fruit. (26)

The fivefold Dharma, which is the cause of both spiritual welfare (śreyas) and worldly prosperity (abhyudaya), has been explained; it should be practiced by persons seeking its fruits, as appropriate to each. (27)
However, in the case of a fully matured girl, the impurity lasts for one year; otherwise, it is three nights.
If she has been betrothed, the impurity lasts for a "two-day" period (pakṣiṇī). ||28||
Thus ends the Dharmaśāstra proclaimed by Pulastya.
